questions.q: An argument's conclusion is
o: what the author wants you to accept
questions.why: Find it first, then judge the support.

questions.q: An assumption is
o: an unstated idea the argument depends on
questions.why: Unstated but needed for the argument to work.

questions.q: What does evaluating evidence involve?
o: Judging its reliability, relevance and sufficiency
questions.why: Examiners (2023): explain why something is a strength or weakness, don't just state it.

questions.q: 'Cities should ban cars from their centres. Air pollution causes thousands of early deaths each year, and cities that have banned cars have cleaner air.' Which is an unstated assumption of this argument?
o: Cities should ban cars from their centres
Some cities have already banned cars
A ban would not simply move the traffic and pollution to other areas
questions.why: The argument needs this to be true but never states it; the other options are a stated reason, the conclusion and stated evidence.

questions.q: An argument claims that because countries with more internet access have higher life expectancy, internet access improves health. What is the main flaw?
o: It assumes correlation shows causation, when wealth may cause both
It does not mention the internet
questions.why: Two things rising together does not prove one causes the other; a third factor such as national income could explain both.

long.q: Read an opinion article on any global issue. Identify its conclusion, two reasons, and one assumption, then evaluate its strength. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a weakness in reasoning or evidence explained

questions.q: Evaluating a perspective means judging
o: the quality of its reasoning and evidence
questions.why: Assess strength, not agreement.

questions.q: How should two perspectives be compared?
o: One after the other with no link
Directly, on the same criteria, with a judgement
questions.why: Examiners (2023): answers without comparison were limited to half marks.

questions.q: Why develop one line of evaluation fully?
o: Depth on one criterion earns more than several undeveloped ones
questions.why: Examiners (2023): this advice recurs for this skills-based syllabus.

questions.q: Perspective A uses data from a large international study; Perspective B relies on one person's story. Which comparison is most valid?
o: B is stronger because personal stories are more truthful
They are equally strong because both are perspectives
A's evidence is more generalisable, though B may show human impacts that the data misses
A is automatically correct because it uses numbers
questions.why: Good evaluation compares the evidence on the same criteria and recognises the strengths and limits of each, rather than accepting or dismissing either outright.

questions.q: A well-argued perspective comes from an organisation funded by the industry it defends. How should this affect your evaluation?
o: Ignore it, because funding never matters
Note the possible vested interest and check whether its evidence is supported elsewhere
Accept it, because it is well argued
questions.why: A vested interest is a reason for caution, not automatic rejection; corroboration shows whether the evidence still holds.

long.q: Perspective A: 'Rich countries produced most past emissions, so they should pay for poorer countries to adapt to climate change.' Perspective B: 'Every country now emits, and aid is often wasted, so each country should pay for its own adaptation.' Compare the strengths and weaknesses of the reasoning and evidence in each perspective, and judge which is more convincing. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a strength of A explained (e.g. historical emissions data support the fairness argument)
B1: a weakness of A explained (e.g. assumes past responsibility passes to today's taxpayers; says nothing about how money is spent)
B1: a strength of B explained (e.g. some emerging economies' current emissions are large and growing)
B1: a weakness of B explained (e.g. 'aid is often wasted' is an unsupported generalisation; ignores the poorest countries' lack of funds)
B1: a supported judgement that follows from the comparison

questions.q: A research question should be
questions.why: It guides the whole essay or report.

questions.q: Which source is usually most credible for a scientific claim?
questions.why: Check the author, expertise, purpose and date.

questions.q: Why suggest further research in an essay?
o: To show awareness of the limits of the evidence used
questions.why: Examiners (2023): more candidates now consider further research.

questions.q: A student's research question is 'Is climate change bad?'. Which revision is the best research question?
o: To what extent should Bangladesh prioritise flood defences over cutting emissions?
questions.why: It is focused, debatable and researchable, inviting evaluation of different perspectives; the others are descriptive, too broad or not questions.

questions.q: Which search strategy is most likely to find credible academic evidence?
o: Searching a scholarly database with specific keywords and checking sources are peer-reviewed
Using the first result from a general search engine
Reading comments under a news article
questions.why: Scholarly databases and peer review give access to expert, checked research, and precise keywords improve relevance.

questions.q: The individual essay must consider
o: different perspectives on a global issue
questions.why: Perspectives are central to the course.

questions.q: How should an essay be written for Questions 2 and 3?
o: In full paragraphs, not bullet points
questions.why: Concise answers are fine only in Question 1.

questions.q: What makes a strong conclusion?
o: A judgement that follows from the evaluation
questions.why: Examiners (2023): judgements were often asserted rather than based on evidence.

questions.q: In an essay on expanding nuclear power, which sentence shows evaluation rather than description?
o: Nuclear power provides about a tenth of the world's electricity.
The safety study covers only European plants, so its findings may not apply to countries with weaker regulation.
Some countries are building new reactors.
Nuclear power is a controversial topic.
questions.why: It judges the limits of the evidence and its relevance, while the others simply state facts.

questions.q: Why should an essay address counter-arguments?
o: To show the judgement has been tested against opposing views, making the conclusion more convincing
Because the counter-argument must always win
questions.why: Weighing opposing perspectives shows balance and makes the final judgement better supported.

questions.q: In the team project, each member
o: researches a different perspective and proposes a solution
does a presentation alone without research
questions.why: Plus an individual reflective paper.

questions.q: What should the reflection in a team project focus on?
o: What was learned, how your view changed and how you'll act differently
questions.why: Examiners (2023): reflections were often descriptive rather than evaluative.

questions.q: In a presentation, what makes slides support the argument?
o: Data and evidence rather than only pictures
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many slides had pictures that offered no support.

questions.q: In the team project, what makes a member's proposed solution to a local issue most convincing?
o: It is the most ambitious idea
It is the member's personal opinion
It copies a solution used elsewhere without change
It is supported by research evidence and is realistic given the different perspectives involved
questions.why: A strong solution follows from the evidence and considers feasibility and the people affected.

questions.q: Which is the most useful reflection on collaboration in the team project?
o: A teammate's research on rural farmers showed me my city-focused solution ignored their needs, so I adapted it.
I did most of the work.
questions.why: It shows how working with others changed the student's own thinking and actions, which is the purpose of reflection.

questions.q: A research report should include
o: a methodology, analysis of sources and a reflective log
questions.why: Method, evidence, judgement and reflection.

questions.q: A research report should be:
o: An argument that answers a question, not a narrative of facts
questions.why: Examiners (2023): reports often lacked argument.

questions.q: Why choose an unusual question for the research report?
o: It allows a fresh argument and avoids over-familiar ground
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many chose very familiar topics.

questions.q: In the Cambridge Research Report, why should the candidate evaluate the methods of the studies they use as evidence?
o: Because the examiner wants a list of methods
Because the strength of the conclusion depends on how reliable and valid that evidence is
Because only primary research is allowed
questions.why: Judging the methods behind the evidence shows how much weight it can bear in answering the question.

questions.q: A draft research report reaches a stronger conclusion than its evidence supports. What should the candidate do?
o: Leave it, as strong conclusions earn more credit
Add more opinions to support it
Qualify the conclusion to match the strength of the evidence and note the limitations
questions.why: A good conclusion is a supported judgement; recognising the limits of the evidence shows critical awareness.
